title: Homemade Electrolyte Drink: Easy DIY Recipe Based on WHO ORS
excerpt: How to make a homemade electrolyte drink with salt, sugar, and water, based on the WHO rehydration formula, plus natural versions, a homemade Pedialyte, and hangover tips.
metaDescription: Make a homemade electrolyte drink with salt, sugar, and water based on the WHO formula. Natural recipes, homemade Pedialyte, and hangover tips.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the best homemade electrolyte drink is also the simplest. Stir **half a level teaspoon of table salt and six level teaspoons of sugar into one liter of clean water** (about 4 1/4 cups), and you have a drink close to the oral rehydration solutions that public health agencies have used for decades to treat dehydration from diarrhea. It costs a few cents, takes a minute, and it works because the salt and sugar are in a specific balance, not because of anything fancy. The two ways people get it wrong are adding too much salt and leaving out the sugar.

**The quick rules:** Measure with real measuring spoons, level them off, and use a full liter of water. Taste it: it should taste about as salty as tears, never like seawater. Sugar is not optional, because it helps your gut pull the sodium and water in. Add potassium from orange juice, coconut water, or a banana on the side. Make a fresh batch every day and keep it in the fridge. For babies, young children, and anyone with kidney, heart, or blood pressure problems, use a store-bought oral rehydration solution and check with a doctor rather than mixing your own.

> **When to see a doctor instead of mixing a drink.** A homemade electrolyte drink is for mild dehydration, such as a hangover, a hot day, or a short stomach bug. **Get medical care if** you can't keep any fluids down for more than several hours, you're vomiting blood or what looks like coffee grounds, you haven't urinated in eight hours or more, you feel faint when you stand, your heart is racing at rest, or you're confused or unusually drowsy. **Call 911** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has blue-tinged or very pale cold skin, or has a seizure. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no drink fixes that. If you drink heavily most days and get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can become dangerous. Talk to a doctor rather than treating it at home.

## Why a Homemade Electrolyte Drink Works: The Salt-and-Sugar Trick

Plain water is great for ordinary thirst. When you've lost a lot of fluid, though, you've also lost salts, mainly sodium and potassium, and your body holds onto water better when those come back too.

The clever part of an electrolyte drink is how the gut absorbs it. The lining of your small intestine has a transporter that carries sodium and glucose across together, one paired with the other, and water follows them in. This is called sodium-glucose co-transport, and it keeps working even when the gut is irritated, which is why oral rehydration became one of the most important medical advances of the twentieth century for treating cholera and childhood diarrhea.

Three things follow from that mechanism:

1. **You need both salt and sugar.** Salt water without sugar is absorbed less efficiently, and a "sugar-free" homemade drink loses the main thing that makes it more than water.
2. **The amounts matter.** Too much sugar or too much salt makes the drink more concentrated than your body fluids, which can pull water *into* the gut and make diarrhea or nausea worse. The goal is a dilute, balanced solution.
3. **More is not better.** A drink that tastes strongly of salt or is syrupy-sweet has missed the point. A good rehydration drink tastes a little flat and a little salty.

## The WHO Oral Rehydration Solution: The Recipe Everything Else Copies

The World Health Organization and UNICEF publish a standard formula for oral rehydration salts, often called ORS. The current version, adopted in the early 2000s, is called "reduced osmolarity" ORS because it is more dilute than the original 1970s formula. Studies found the more dilute version caused less vomiting and shorter bouts of diarrhea in children.

Per liter of water, the WHO formula contains:

| Ingredient | Amount per liter | What it supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Sodium chloride (table salt) | 2.6 g | Sodium and chloride |
| Glucose (anhydrous) | 13.5 g | Fuel for sodium absorption |
| Potassium chloride | 1.5 g | Potassium |
| Trisodium citrate, dihydrate | 2.9 g | Corrects acid build-up |

Those amounts are precise because the packets are made in factories with lab scales. At home you won't have potassium chloride and trisodium citrate in the pantry, and that's fine. The simplified sugar-salt solution covers the two parts that do most of the work, sodium and sugar, and you can add potassium from food.

A useful way to think about it: the WHO packet is the gold standard, a store-bought rehydration drink such as Pedialyte is a close cousin designed for the same job, and a carefully measured homemade drink is a decent stand-in when you don't have either.

## The Basic DIY Electrolyte Drink Recipe (Sugar-Salt Solution)

This is the version public health groups have taught for years for use at home.

**You need:**

- 1 liter (about 4 1/4 cups) of clean drinking water, boiled and cooled if your tap water isn't safe to drink
- 1/2 level teaspoon of table salt
- 6 level teaspoons of white sugar (2 level tablespoons)

**Steps:**

1. Pour the water into a clean jug or bottle. Measure it. Guessing the liter is the most common mistake.
2. Add the salt and sugar using measuring spoons, leveled off with a knife. A heaped teaspoon can hold nearly double the salt.
3. Stir or shake until everything dissolves completely.
4. Taste it. It should taste no saltier than tears. If it tastes clearly salty, pour some out and add more water.
5. Chill it if you like. Cold drinks are often easier to sip when you feel queasy.

**What's in it, roughly:** half a teaspoon of table salt is around 3 grams, which supplies a little over 1,000 mg of sodium across the whole liter. Six teaspoons of sugar is around 25 grams. That puts the drink in the same general range as medical rehydration drinks: much less sugar than soda or juice, and much more sodium than a typical sports drink.

**How to drink it:** sip, don't chug. Small, frequent sips are easier on an upset stomach. If you vomit, wait 10 to 15 minutes and start again with smaller sips.

## How to Make an Electrolyte Drink With Potassium

The basic recipe has no potassium. For a hangover or a hot day that's usually not a big deal, because a normal meal restores it. But if you've lost fluid for a while, or you just want something closer to the WHO formula, here are easy ways to add it.

**Option 1: Orange juice swap.** Replace about 1/2 cup of the water with orange juice. Orange juice is naturally rich in potassium and adds some flavor. Because juice has its own sugar, cut the added sugar to about 4 to 5 level teaspoons.

**Option 2: Eat potassium on the side.** Drink the basic sugar-salt solution and eat a banana, a potato, a bowl of yogurt, or some avocado. Food is a perfectly good way to replace potassium, and it's harder to overdo than adding powders. Bananas come up a lot as a hangover food for exactly this reason.

**Option 3: A pinch of "lite" salt.** Some salt substitutes and "lite" salts contain potassium chloride. Swapping part of the table salt for one of these adds potassium. Be careful here: potassium supplements and salt substitutes can be dangerous for people with kidney disease and for anyone taking medicines that raise potassium, including some blood pressure drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and potassium-sparing diuretics). If that's you, skip this option and ask your doctor.

## Natural Electrolyte Drink Recipes (Without Table Sugar)

Plenty of people search for a "natural" version. You can make one, as long as you remember that the drink still needs some form of sugar to work, and that natural ingredients vary a lot from batch to batch.

### Honey-Lemon Electrolyte Drink

- 1 liter of water
- 1/2 level teaspoon of salt
- 2 level tablespoons of honey (dissolve it in a little warm water first)
- Juice of 1 lemon or 2 limes

Honey is mostly glucose and fructose, so it can stand in for table sugar. **Never give honey to babies under one year old**, because of the risk of infant botulism.

### Coconut Water Electrolyte Drink

- 2 cups of plain, unsweetened coconut water
- 2 cups of water
- 1/4 level teaspoon of salt
- Squeeze of lime, optional

Coconut water has plenty of potassium but relatively little sodium, so on its own it isn't a complete rehydration drink. Cutting it with water and adding a small amount of salt brings it closer to balanced. Its natural sugar is usually enough, so taste before adding any more. We cover the pros and cons in more detail in [coconut water for hangovers](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover).

### Ginger Electrolyte Drink for a Queasy Stomach

- 1 liter of weak ginger tea (a few slices of fresh ginger steeped in hot water), cooled
- 1/2 level teaspoon of salt
- 2 level tablespoons of honey or 6 level teaspoons of sugar

Ginger has reasonable evidence for easing some kinds of nausea, and many people find it easier to keep down than plain salt water. Serve it cold.

### Watermelon or Fruit-Juice Variation

Blend 2 cups of watermelon, strain it, and add enough water to make a liter, plus 1/2 teaspoon of salt. Watermelon gives you water, some potassium, and natural sugar. Fruit varies, so taste: if it's very sweet, add more water rather than more salt.

**What about sugar-free?** If you're avoiding sugar for everyday sports or hydration, a lightly salted water with lemon can be fine for someone who is just a bit thirsty. But for actual rehydration after vomiting or diarrhea, there is no good evidence that a sugar-free homemade drink works as well, because it skips the sodium-glucose pairing that makes ORS effective. People with diabetes should talk to their doctor about which rehydration product to use when they're sick.

## Homemade Pedialyte: How Close Can You Get?

"Homemade Pedialyte" is one of the most searched versions of this question. Here's the honest comparison.

Pedialyte and similar products are built on the same principle as the WHO formula: a measured amount of sodium, potassium, chloride, and sugar, plus citrate, made to consistent standards. The classic unflavored version is in the same general range as the WHO solution for sodium, potassium, and sugar, which is why doctors often recommend it for kids with stomach bugs.

A homemade sugar-salt drink with orange juice or a banana on the side gets you most of the way there. What you give up:

- **Precision.** Measuring spoons and natural ingredients vary. A factory doesn't.
- **Citrate.** Commercial products include it to help correct the mild acid build-up that comes with significant dehydration. A home drink usually doesn't.
- **Safety margin for small children.** A small child is much more sensitive to a mixing error than an adult.

For an adult with a hangover, homemade is a sensible, cheap option. For a baby or toddler who is sick, use a store-bought rehydration solution and call your pediatrician. If you want to compare the commercial options directly, see [Pedialyte vs Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) and our roundup of [electrolyte drinks for a hangover compared](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).

## Homemade Electrolyte Drink vs Sports Drinks, Pedialyte, and Liquid I.V.

| Drink | Sodium | Sugar | Potassium | Best use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Homemade sugar-salt solution | Moderate to high | Low to moderate | None unless added | Cheap rehydration at home |
| WHO oral rehydration salts | Moderate to high | Low | Yes | Diarrhea and real dehydration |
| Pedialyte (classic) | Moderate to high | Low | Yes | Kids' stomach bugs, hangovers |
| Electrolyte powders like Liquid I.V. | Moderate to high | Varies by version | Yes | Convenience, travel |
| Standard sports drinks | Low | Higher | Low | Fueling long exercise |
| Plain water | None | None | None | Everyday thirst |

Sports drinks are designed mainly to deliver carbohydrates and some fluid during long exercise, so they tend to have more sugar and noticeably less sodium than rehydration solutions. They're fine if that's what you have, and you can water them down a little and add a pinch of salt to move them closer to a rehydration drink. Packaged powders are more convenient than homemade, and some are close to ORS in sodium, but you pay for that convenience.

The homemade version wins on cost and on knowing exactly what's in it. It loses on convenience and consistency.

## Homemade Electrolyte Drink for a Hangover: What It Can and Can't Do

This is where a homemade electrolyte drink earns its place for most of our readers, and also where it's worth being honest about its limits.

**Why alcohol dries you out.** Alcohol lowers the release of vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. With less of it around, you urinate more than you drink. That's why you make repeated trips to the bathroom after a few drinks. If you also sweat on a dance floor, sleep in a warm room, or throw up, you lose more fluid and some sodium and potassium along with it.

**What an electrolyte drink helps with.** Dry mouth, thirst, lightheadedness when you stand up, and the part of a headache that comes from being low on fluid can all improve as you rehydrate. If you've been vomiting, a sugar-salt drink sipped slowly is one of the gentlest ways to get fluid back in.

**What it doesn't fix.** A hangover is more than dehydration. Researchers who study hangovers point to several other causes: inflammation, poor sleep, acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol), low blood sugar, and irritation of the stomach lining. Reviews of hangover research have also noted that measured electrolyte levels in hungover people don't track closely with how bad they feel. So rehydrating can take the edge off, but there is no good evidence that electrolyte drinks prevent or cure a hangover on their own. For other drinks worth considering the morning after, see [the best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks).

**Timing.** The most useful moments to drink a glass are before bed and first thing in the morning. A glass between alcoholic drinks also helps you drink less overall, which does more for the next morning than any recipe. For a fuller look at timing, see [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).

### A Simple Morning-After Plan

1. Start with a glass of your homemade electrolyte drink, sipped over 15 to 20 minutes.
2. Eat something easy: toast, eggs, a banana, or soup. Food brings back blood sugar and potassium. Our guide to [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains why eggs are a popular choice.
3. Keep sipping water or the electrolyte drink through the morning. Aim for pale yellow urine.
4. Skip the extra coffee if your stomach is upset, or pair it with water.
5. If nausea is the main problem, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more ideas.

## How Much Homemade Electrolyte Drink Should You Drink?

For a healthy adult with mild dehydration, like a hangover or a hot afternoon, one to two liters spread over the day is a reasonable amount, along with normal food and water. You don't need to finish a full liter in one sitting.

Watch your body rather than a number. Signs you're rehydrating well include urinating every few hours, urine turning pale yellow, less thirst, and no more lightheadedness when you stand up.

There are two reasons not to overdo it:

- **Salt adds up.** A liter of the basic recipe contains a meaningful share of a day's recommended sodium. That's fine for a day of rehydration, but it's not something to drink every day in place of water, especially if you have high blood pressure.
- **Too much fluid is possible.** It's rare, but drinking very large amounts of any fluid quickly can lower blood sodium. Rehydration drinks are less likely to cause this than plain water because they contain sodium, but sipping steadily is still the right approach.

## Common Mistakes When Making DIY Electrolyte Drinks

- **Using too much salt.** This is the big one. A heaped spoon, a tablespoon instead of a teaspoon, or too little water can all make the drink saltier than your body fluids, which can worsen thirst, nausea, or diarrhea. If it tastes salty like soup, dilute it.
- **Leaving out the sugar.** Without sugar the drink works much more like slightly salty water.
- **Using too much sugar.** Juice or soda as the base, or extra sweetener "for taste," turns it into a sugary drink that can make diarrhea worse.
- **Guessing the water.** A liter is about 4 1/4 US cups. A large drinking glass is often only 1 1/2 cups.
- **Keeping it too long.** Homemade drinks have no preservatives. Refrigerate and use within 24 hours, then make a new batch.
- **Using untreated water.** If you wouldn't drink the tap water, boil it and cool it first.
- **Adding "extra" minerals at random.** Magnesium powders, potassium supplements, and baking soda can all upset the balance. Stick to the tested recipes unless a clinician tells you otherwise.

## Who Should Use a Store-Bought Solution Instead

A homemade drink is fine for most healthy adults, but these groups should use a commercial oral rehydration solution and get medical advice:

- **Babies and young children.** They dehydrate quickly and are more sensitive to mixing errors. Call your pediatrician for a sick infant.
- **People with kidney disease, heart failure, or liver disease.** Sodium and potassium balance can be tricky, and the right fluid plan may be different.
- **People on medications that affect salt or potassium.** This includes many blood pressure medicines and diuretics ("water pills").
- **People with diabetes.** The sugar in rehydration drinks matters, and so does keeping blood sugar steady when you're sick.
- **Older adults who are already frail or unwell.** Dehydration can escalate faster.
- **Anyone who is getting worse instead of better.** If symptoms aren't improving after a day, or you have signs of serious dehydration, see a doctor.

## Can You Prevent the Dehydration in the First Place?

You can make it a lot smaller. A few habits do most of the work:

- **Alternate drinks.** Have a glass of water or a light electrolyte drink between alcoholic drinks.
- **Eat before and while drinking.** Food slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream. See [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide).
- **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, though this varies from person to person.
- **Have a glass before bed.** Keep your homemade drink in the fridge so it's waiting for you.

For the bigger picture, our [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) guide puts these habits in order of how much they help.

## Where DHM Fits Alongside an Electrolyte Drink

Electrolyte drinks deal with fluid and salt. They don't do anything about how your body processes alcohol itself. That's the part some people try to support with **dihydromyricetin (DHM)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree.

To be clear about the evidence: the studies on DHM, alcohol metabolism and the brain were done in rats, mice and cell cultures, and no published trial has paired DHM with an electrolyte drink. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers, and it isn't a substitute for drinking less, eating, or rehydrating. Some people choose to take it before or while drinking as one part of a routine that also includes water and an electrolyte drink before bed.

If you want to try it, two options we've reviewed are [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a straightforward single-ingredient option, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with other ingredients and some electrolytes. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when. If you take prescription medicines, check with a doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

A homemade electrolyte drink is one of the cheapest, most useful things you can keep in your fridge. Half a level teaspoon of salt and six level teaspoons of sugar in one liter of clean water gives you a drink close to the WHO rehydration formula, and you can add potassium with orange juice, coconut water, or a banana on the side. Measure carefully, sip slowly, and make a fresh batch each day.

For a hangover, it can help with thirst, lightheadedness, and the dehydration part of a headache. It won't fix poor sleep, inflammation, or the other things that make the morning after rough, so pair it with food, rest, and drinking less the night before. And if you can't keep fluids down, feel faint, or someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, skip the kitchen and get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How do you make a homemade electrolyte drink?**

Mix half a level teaspoon of table salt and six level teaspoons of sugar into one liter (about 4 1/4 cups) of clean drinking water, and stir until dissolved. This simple sugar-salt solution is modeled on the WHO oral rehydration formula. It should taste no saltier than tears. Use measuring spoons, level them off, and make a fresh batch every day.

**What is the WHO oral rehydration solution recipe?**

The WHO's reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration salts contain, per liter of water, 2.6 g sodium chloride, 13.5 g glucose, 1.5 g potassium chloride, and 2.9 g trisodium citrate. At home, the simplified version is half a level teaspoon of salt and six level teaspoons of sugar per liter, with potassium added from orange juice, coconut water, or food such as a banana.

**Why does a homemade electrolyte drink need sugar?**

The gut absorbs sodium and glucose together through a shared transporter, and water follows them in. Without sugar, the drink is absorbed more like slightly salty water. The amount matters too: a small amount helps, but too much sugar can pull water into the gut and make diarrhea or nausea worse.

**Is a homemade electrolyte drink as good as Pedialyte?**

For a healthy adult with mild dehydration, such as a hangover, a carefully measured homemade drink gets you most of the way there for a few cents. Commercial products are more precise and include citrate and potassium. For babies, young children, and people with kidney, heart, or blood pressure problems, use a store-bought oral rehydration solution and check with a doctor.

**Does a homemade electrolyte drink help a hangover?**

It can help with the dehydration part: thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and some of the headache. Alcohol lowers vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you lose more fluid than you drink. But hangovers also involve poor sleep, inflammation, and acetaldehyde, and there is no good evidence that electrolyte drinks prevent or cure a hangover on their own.

**What is the best natural electrolyte drink?**

A honey-lemon version (1 liter water, half a teaspoon of salt, 2 tablespoons of honey, juice of a lemon) or a coconut water version (2 cups unsweetened coconut water, 2 cups water, a quarter teaspoon of salt) both work well. Coconut water is high in potassium but low in sodium, so it needs the added salt. Never give honey to babies under one year old.

**How long does a homemade electrolyte drink last?**

Keep it in the fridge and use it within 24 hours. Homemade drinks have no preservatives, so throw out what's left after a day and make a new batch. If your tap water isn't safe to drink, boil it and let it cool before mixing.

**Can you make an electrolyte drink without sugar?**

You can make lightly salted water with lemon for everyday thirst, but for real rehydration after vomiting or diarrhea there is no good evidence a sugar-free homemade drink works as well, because it skips the sodium-glucose pairing that makes oral rehydration effective. If you have diabetes, ask your doctor which rehydration product to use when you're sick.

**When should I see a doctor instead of using an electrolyte drink?**

Get care if you can't keep fluids down for more than several hours, haven't urinated in eight hours or more, feel faint when standing, are confused, or are vomiting blood. Call 911 if someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, or has a seizure, as these are signs of alcohol poisoning.
